title: Positioning and Stacking Contexts
summary: The position property decides both what an element removes from normal flow and what it's anchored against. Stacking contexts explain why z-index sometimes silently refuses to work — and it isn't the z-index value that's wrong.

slides.markdown:
`position` answers two separate questions at once: does this element stay in normal flow, and what is it anchored relative to. Get the anchor wrong and an element that looks correctly positioned in one layout jumps to a completely different spot when a parent's CSS changes.

The second half of this topic is the bug almost every frontend developer hits at least once: setting `z-index: 9999` on an element and watching it still render *behind* something else. That isn't a z-index problem — it's a **stacking context** problem, and z-index values only compete within the same context.

Both pieces — positioning and stacking — build directly on the box model from the previous topic: a positioned element is still a box with content/padding/border/margin, just relocated.

slides.subTitle: What each removes from flow
slides.markdown:
- **`static`** (default): normal flow, `top`/`left`/`right`/`bottom` have no effect.
- **`relative`**: stays in normal flow — its original space is preserved — but can be nudged with `top`/`left`/etc, offset from where it would otherwise sit.
- **`absolute`**: removed from flow entirely. Sibling elements act as if it doesn't exist. Positioned relative to its nearest *positioned* ancestor (see next slide).
- **`fixed`**: removed from flow, positioned relative to the viewport (or the nearest ancestor with a `transform`/`filter`/`will-change`, a frequent gotcha).
- **`sticky`**: hybrid — behaves like `relative` until a scroll threshold, then switches to acting like `fixed` within its containing block.

The flow-removal question sorts cleanly into two groups: `static` and `relative` stay in flow (`relative` just visually offsets); `absolute` and `fixed` leave flow completely. `sticky` is the odd one that changes behavior based on scroll position.

slides.subTitle: Nudging vs anchoring
slides.markdown:
`relative` does two unrelated jobs, and conflating them is a common source of confusion.

**Job 1 — nudging**: `position: relative; top: 10px` shifts the element visually by 10px from where normal flow would place it, while its original space stays reserved (nothing else moves in to fill the gap).

**Job 2 — anchoring**: `position: relative` on a container, with **no offset at all**, creates a *positioning context* for any `absolute` descendant. That descendant will now anchor to this container's edges instead of drifting up to the nearest positioned ancestor further up the tree (or the viewport, if none exists).

In practice, job 2 is the far more common reason to write `position: relative` — a card component with an absolutely-positioned badge in its corner needs `position: relative` on the card purely so the badge anchors to the card, not the page. No visual nudging happens; the `relative` here is invisible until you add the absolute child.

`position: sticky` looks simple — "stick to the top while scrolling" — but breaks in three predictable ways:

- **A parent with `overflow: hidden`, `auto`, or `scroll`.** Sticky positioning is scoped to its nearest scrolling ancestor, not the page. If any ancestor clips or scrolls independently, the sticky element sticks *within that ancestor's box*, not the viewport — and if that ancestor is shorter than the viewport, the sticky element may never appear to stick at all.
- **Missing a threshold value.** `position: sticky` with no `top` (or `bottom`/`left`/`right`) does nothing — the browser needs at least one offset to know when to "trigger" sticking.
- **A container shorter than the sticky element itself.** Sticky only sticks *within its parent's height*. If the parent is exactly the sticky element's height, there's no scroll room for it to look stuck — it simply scrolls normally.

The fix for the first case is almost always the same: remove the unnecessary `overflow` from an intermediate wrapper, or restructure so the scrolling container is the one you actually want sticky to be scoped to.

slides.subTitle: What creates one, and why z-index "doesn't work"
slides.markdown:
z-index only compares elements **within the same stacking context**. If two elements live in different contexts, the *context's* stacking order wins before any child z-index is even considered — no child z-index value, however large, can escape its parent context.

A stacking context is created by, among others: any positioned element (`relative`/`absolute`/`fixed`/`sticky`) with a `z-index` other than `auto`, any element with `opacity < 1`, `transform`, `filter`, or `will-change` set, and the root element itself.

The classic trap: element A has `z-index: 9999` but its parent has `opacity: 0.99` (creating a new stacking context for everything inside it). Element B, outside that parent, has `z-index: 2`. B still renders on top, because B is comparing against the *parent's* stacking position in the outer context — A's 9999 only wins fights against its own siblings inside the same parent.

It helps to stop thinking of z-index as a single flat number line and instead picture a **tree of contexts**, each with its own local ordering.

At the root, siblings stack by their z-index (or source order if `auto`). Any sibling that creates its own stacking context becomes a single "folder" in that ordering — everything inside it stacks *relative to each other*, then the whole folder is placed as one unit among its own siblings. A z-index of 9999 set two folders deep can never outrank a folder-level z-index of 1 at the level above it, because the comparison never crosses folder boundaries directly — it resolves folder-vs-folder first, then descends.

slides.sectionTitle: A sticky header and dropdown fighting over z-index

slides.subTitle: Choosing for common UI patterns
slides.markdown:
| Pattern | Right choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Header that stays visible while scrolling the whole page | `fixed` | Anchored to viewport, indifferent to page length |
| Table-of-contents header that pins once you scroll past it | `sticky` | Should scroll normally at first, then pin — `fixed` would pin from page load |
| Tooltip/badge anchored to one specific card | `absolute` (with `relative` on the card) | Needs to move with its own container, not the viewport |
| Modal overlay covering the whole screen | `fixed` | Must stay centered regardless of scroll position |
| Sidebar nav that scrolls away with content on mobile, pins on desktop | `sticky` inside a media query, or `static`/`fixed` toggled | Behavior genuinely differs by viewport |

The fast mental filter: if it should ever be scrollable-then-pin, it's `sticky`. If it should never move regardless of scroll, it's `fixed`. If it should move with one specific ancestor, it's `absolute` with `relative` on that ancestor.

When z-index "isn't working," the productive question isn't "is my z-index high enough" — it's "what stacking context is this element actually competing inside."

A practical process: open DevTools, and in Chrome's Layers panel or Firefox's 3D view, inspect which elements are creating stacking contexts (both panels flag them explicitly). Walk up from the misbehaving element until you find the ancestor with `opacity`, `transform`, `filter`, or a positioned `z-index` that's boxing it in. Then decide: remove that property if it's not load-bearing, or move the element out of that subtree (portal/teleport pattern in React/Vue), or raise the *ancestor's* z-index instead of the child's.

Raising only the child's z-index almost never fixes a cross-context conflict — it's the single most common wasted debugging step, because it looks like it should work and silently does nothing.

slides.sectionTitle: Positioned elements and the box model
slides.markdown:
A positioned element doesn't get a different box — content/padding/border/margin still apply exactly as covered in the previous topic. What changes is only *where the box's position is calculated from* and *whether it participates in flow*.

One interaction worth knowing: percentage-based `top`/`left`/`width`/`height` on an `absolute` element resolve against the **padding box** of its nearest positioned ancestor, not the ancestor's content box or margin box. That's a frequent source of off-by-a-few-pixels bugs when an ancestor has padding — the absolute child's percentage sizing includes that padding in its reference dimensions in ways that surprise people who assume it matches the content area exactly.

Positioning is a targeted escape hatch for one-off placement — a tooltip, a modal, a sticky header. It is not a general layout tool: stacking a full page of content with `absolute` positioning quickly becomes unmanageable, because nothing auto-adjusts to its siblings' sizes.

That's exactly the gap flexbox and grid (next two topics) fill: distributing space among many siblings automatically, without manual pixel math or worrying about stacking-context side effects, since flex/grid items don't create implicit stacking surprises the way transformed or opacity-adjusted positioned elements do.
